title: Revered in the Community, Frustrating in Schools: A Cree Backward Spirit in Canadian Public Education
content: In the land now known as Canada, the Indian Act was put into place to control and assimilate First Nations people. Well-established First Nations systems for education and health were replaced with Indian Residential Schools and Western systems, where racist stereotypes prevail. The purpose of this study was to better understand the experience of Indigenous caregivers with psychological assessment and diagnosis of their child. The research questions pertained to caregiver experiences with (1) having their child assessed and diagnosed, and (2) navigating services post-diagnosis. In-terpretative phenomenological analysis was used to learn about the experiences of Indigenous caregivers, and this article elucidates the experience of one First Nations mother. The main findings are that Indigenous caregivers experience similar stressors when interacting with systems as other parents, including strained relationships, difficulty with communication, myriad emotions, and constrained resources. Additionally, Indigenous caregivers may experience differences in worldview regarding disability and may encounter compounding barriers due to Indigenous ex-periences, such as racist assumptions and treatment of the child and caregivers. The main conclu-sion is that Indigenous worldviews regarding the construct of disability and Indigenous experiences in North American society should be taken into consideration when planning responsive services.
